exam: A patient presents 3 weeks after pelvic radiotherapy with watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramping — differentiate radiation enteritis from infectious colitis and outline immediate management — identify timing, lack of fever, and supportive care with antidiarrheals and nutrition.

You notice grade 3 skin erythema and ulceration in a patient receiving head‑and‑neck radiotherapy — what grading system do you use and how does it guide treatment — apply CTCAE grading, start topical steroids and consider treatment break.

A child treated for Hodgkin lymphoma develops cough and low‑grade fever 5 weeks post‑RT — what diagnosis is most likely and what is the first therapeutic step — suspect radiation pneumonitis, obtain chest X‑ray, start oral steroids promptly.

During radiotherapy for cervical cancer a patient with known HIV develops severe mucositis — which drug class should be avoided and why — avoid additional myelosuppressive chemotherapy as it would worsen bone‑marrow toxicity.

A patient on concurrent chemoradiation presents with neutrophil count 0.8 ×10⁹/L — what is the next action and what monitoring is required — hold chemotherapy, give infection prophylaxis, monitor temperature and repeat CBC daily.

You are in a low‑resource hospital without CT; a patient after thoracic radiotherapy has new leg weakness — what emergency condition must you rule out and how — suspect spinal cord compression; perform urgent neurological exam and arrange transfer for MRI if possible.

Explain why fractionating a total dose of 60 Gy into 2 Gy fractions reduces late fibrosis compared with 3 Gy fractions — smaller daily doses allow normal tissue DNA repair, lowering cumulative damage.

A patient complains of persistent dry mouth 1 year after head‑and‑neck radiotherapy — what late toxicity is this and what supportive measure can be offered — xerostomia; advise saliva substitutes and good oral hygiene.
ai.title: Radiation Toxicity
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Radiation toxicity describes tissue injury from therapeutic ionising radiation. Severity depends on dose, fractionation, tissue type and patient factors, and it can present acutely or months later.

b: Acute toxicity: skin erythema, mucositis, nausea, bone marrow suppression.
Late toxicity: fibrosis, vascular injury, organ dysfunction.
sections.p: Therapeutic radiation damages DNA and generates free radicals, leading to cell death and inflammation. Early effects occur within weeks, while late effects may appear years after exposure.

b: Total dose (Gy) and fraction size are the main determinants of toxicity.
Concurrent chemotherapy amplifies radiation injury.
Patient factors: HIV, malnutrition, prior irradiation increase risk.
sections.p: Radiation tolerance varies: rapidly dividing tissues (skin, gut, bone marrow) are most sensitive, while nerve and muscle tolerate higher doses. Fractionation allows normal tissue repair between doses.

b: Identify early signs to prevent progression.
Know which toxicities require urgent intervention (e.g., spinal cord compression).
Tailor follow‑up when imaging or labs are limited.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, many cancers are treated with external beam radiotherapy without advanced planning tools, raising the risk of avoidable toxicity.

t.b: What is the extent and grade of skin or mucosal injury? – Grading (CTCAE) guides management; if unavailable, use descriptive severity (mild, moderate, severe).
Is there bone‑marrow suppression? – Low neutrophils or platelets indicate need for infection prophylaxis or transfusion; if lab unavailable, monitor for fever and bleeding.
Are electrolytes or renal function impaired by nephrotoxic radiation? – Abnormalities guide fluid and medication adjustments; if unavailable, assess urine output and clinical signs.
Is there organ fibrosis or fluid collection? – Detects pleural effusion, bowel obstruction; if imaging not possible, rely on clinical exam (e.g., decreased breath sounds).

b: Skin: gentle cleansing, topical steroids for grade ≥2, avoid friction.
Mucositis: oral hygiene, saline rinses, topical anesthetics; consider systemic analgesia.
Bone‑marrow suppression: infection prophylaxis, transfusion if needed, avoid myelosuppressive drugs.
Fibrosis: physiotherapy, anti‑fibrotic agents (e.g., pentoxifylline) when available.
sections.p: Treat the underlying radiation effect, provide symptomatic care, and monitor for progression.

b: Radiation pneumonitis vs. bacterial pneumonia – timing (2‑6 weeks post‑RT) and lack of fever suggest radiation.
Radiation enteritis vs. infectious colitis – presence of prior pelvic irradiation and chronicity favour radiation.
sections.p: Radiation toxicity can mimic infection, chemotherapy toxicity, or disease progression.

b: Normal CBC early in acute marrow suppression; repeat testing if symptoms evolve.
X‑ray may miss early fibrosis; clinical assessment remains crucial.
sections.p: Laboratory and imaging findings may be normal early despite severe tissue injury.

b: Describe CTCAE grading for skin toxicity.
Explain why fractionation reduces late toxicity.
Identify red‑flag signs needing urgent referral (e.g., spinal cord compression).
sections.p: Examiners test integration of pathophysiology, recognition, and management.

b: Assuming all erythema is infection – consider radiation grade.
Delaying steroids for radiation pneumonitis – early treatment improves outcome.
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from under‑recognising delayed effects or over‑relying on unavailable tests.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dyspnoea or neurological deficit suggesting spinal cord compression
